## Selecting versus Evaluating

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Module 7 scored every setting of a grid on the six tuning projects and took the best. The winner's score is optimistic. The same six projects chose the winner and then graded it. Among many settings, the best score owes something to luck.

The final test on HOLZ is honest, because the setting was fixed before HOLZ was scored. Yet it rests on a single project of 26 study effects, and its interval is wide. Nested LOGO-CV offers a second route, which spends no project on the test alone.

The two routes answer different questions [@pargent2023], and a third question has no answer:

| question | answered by |
|:--|:--|
| What is a fixed setting worth on a new project? | LOGO-CV (Module 6), or a final test (Listing 35) |
| What is the procedure "search the grid, fit the winner" worth on a new project? | Nested LOGO-CV (Listing 36) |
| What is the winning setting worth, judged by the projects that chose it? | Not answerable: those projects are spent |

Listing 36 writes the outer loop of the nested search out by hand on the 18 settings of Listing 33, so that it runs in about 15 minutes. Each inner search picks its winner by `lower`, the rule of Module 7. The package ships the same search over the full grid of 1,320 settings as the dataset `nested`, which took about 140 minutes on four cores.
:::

## Nested LOGO-CV

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Nested LOGO-CV runs the whole of Module 7 seven times, once with each project removed. With a project set aside, the grid search of Listing 34 runs on the other six, picks a winner, the winner is refit on those six, and the set-aside project is scored once. Seven numbers come out, each from a model whose setting was chosen without the project it is scored on. That is what the final test on HOLZ did once; nesting does it for every project, so no project is spent on the test alone.

The numbers answer a different question than Listing 34's winner. The winner's six estimates are optimistic, because the same six folds chose it among 18 and then graded it: the best of 18 noisy scores is biased upward. The nested estimates carry no such selection, so they say what the procedure "search this grid, fit the winner" is worth on a new project. They say nothing about any one setting, and the seven winners chosen along the way show how much the choice varies; they are not candidates.

On our data, the run shows two things. The choice is unstable: the seven searches picked five different settings, and the winner of Listing 34 only twice. The optimism is small: the winner's mean over the six tuning projects is 0.78, and the nested mean over the same six is 0.77, a difference of about 0.01. That is far inside the spread across projects, 0.64 to 1.00. With a coarse grid of similar settings there is little to overfit, and the spread across projects, not the tuning, limits the estimate. Nested searches commonly pick by the plain mean, without the SD, and `sort_by = "mean"` does that. We ran both rules: over all seven projects, the nested means were 0.77 by the mean and 0.76 by `lower`, a difference below 0.01.
:::

#### Listing 36

Run a nested leave-one-group-out cross-validation (about 15 minutes).

```{r listing-36}
# The seven projects, HOLZ included: each is held out once
proj_all <- sort(unique(df$pid))

# The AUROC of each held-out project, and the setting its search chose
auc_nested_diy <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(proj_all)), proj_all)
winners_diy <- list()

runtime_nested <- system.time({
  # Outer loop: each project is held out once and scored once
  for (rp in proj_all) {
    # Progress report, overwritten in place
    cat("\rHeld-out project:", rp)
    # The held-out project leaves the data, so the search cannot see it
    train_cv <- df[df$pid != rp, ]
    # Inner loop: the grid search of Listing 34 on the other six projects
    inner <- tune_logo_cv(
      ada_fit,
      ada_hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")],
      data = train_cv,
      group = "pid"
    )
    # The winner: the highest lower over the inner folds, the rule of Module 7
    winners_diy[[rp]] <- summary(inner, "auroc", sort_by = "lower")[
      1,
      c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")
    ]
    # The pipeline of Listing 34 at the winning setting: trained on the
    # six projects, scored once on the held-out one
    logo_rp <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train_cv[, voi_nms],
      method = "class",
      maxdepth = winners_diy[[rp]]$depth,
      parms = list(split = "gini"),
      model = TRUE
    ) |>
      adaboost(
        n_iter = winners_diy[[rp]]$n_iter,
        eta = winners_diy[[rp]]$eta,
        verbose = FALSE
      ) |>
      logo_cv(data = df, group = "pid", holdout = rp)
    auc_nested_diy[[rp]] <- logo_rp$estimates[1, rp, "auroc"]
  }
})

# Run time in minutes
runtime_nested[["elapsed"]] / 60

# The nested estimates, one per project
auc_nested_diy |> round(2)

# The setting each search chose
do.call(rbind, winners_diy)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Listing 36 wraps one more loop around the search of Listing 34. The outer loop takes each of the seven projects in turn, HOLZ included, and removes it from the data, so nothing inside the loop can see it. The inner loop is the grid search of Listing 34, run by `tune_logo_cv()` on the remaining six projects. `summary()` ranks the 18 settings by `lower` over the six inner folds, the rule of Module 7, and its first row is the winner. The winner then runs through the pipeline of Listing 34, where `logo_cv()` with `holdout = rp` trains it on the six projects and scores the held-out project once. The loop runs seven grid searches on one core and took about 15 minutes. Appendix E writes the same search out with every step by hand.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Changed since submission"}
- New listing (R1.C11.a): the outer loop of nested LOGO-CV around the grid search of Listing 34 (submitted: none). The inner search is `tune_logo_cv()`, and its winner is the first row of `summary()` sorted by `lower`, the rule of Module 7. The winner is refitted with the pipeline of Listing 34 and scored through `logo_cv()` with `holdout`.
:::

#### The Package Solution [NEW]

Run the same nested cross-validation with adatutor on four cores (about 6 minutes).

```{r listing-36-pkg}
# The nested search in one call
ada_nested <- tune_logo_cv(
  ada_fit,
  ada_hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")],
  data = df,
  group = "pid",
  nested = TRUE,
  metric = "auroc",
  sort_by = "lower",
  cores = 4
)

# One estimate per project, with the setting its search chose
ada_nested

# The seven estimates in one row
summary(ada_nested)

# Verification: the seven estimates of Listing 36, matched by project
all.equal(
  ada_nested$estimates[proj_all, "auroc"],
  auc_nested_diy
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
`tune_logo_cv()` with `nested = TRUE` does what Listing 36 does in one call: for each project, a grid search on the other six, the winner by `sort_by = "lower"` on `metric = "auroc"`, and one score on the held-out project. Its printout names this rule in the header, lists each held-out project with the setting its search chose and its estimate, and counts the distinct settings the inner searches chose. With `cores = 4`, it spreads the work over four cores and took about 6 minutes, against about 15 minutes for Listing 36. Readers who do not want to wait for Listing 36 can run this call instead. The two match, so we continue with the package function: it keeps the listings short and saves typing. Readers who prefer their own code can continue with Listing 36.

`summary()` condenses the seven estimates into the statistics of Module 7: a mean of 0.76, an SD of 0.13, and a `lower` of 0.63.
:::

# Where to go next

## Next algorithm

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (box, decide at port)"}

The cross-validation part goes pretty far, but the finess of the algorithm is limited. But nothing holds more advanced reader to explore the worflow in a diy fashion or use, xgb with our package.

**XGBoost by the same workflow.** XGBoost has `logo_cv()` and `tune_logo_cv()` methods as well, nesting included, so this box runs the nested search of Module 9 on a grid of XGBoost's own. The grid crosses depths 1, 2 and 4, learning rates 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01, `min_child_weight` 1 and 5, `lambda` 1 and 10, and 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1,000 rounds. That makes 180 settings. The fit from `xgboost::xgboost()` is the recipe. It keeps no formula, so `outcome` names the outcome column. As for AdaBoost, the settings that differ only in their rounds share one fit per fold, and the shorter fits are read off it. XGBoost has a rule of its own, not the highest `lower` of Module 7: the best worst project, with ties broken by `lower`. `sort_by = c("min", "lower")` hands this rule to every inner search. The nested call holds out each of the seven projects in turn, searches the grid on the other six, refits the pick on them, and scores the held-out project once. The HOLZ fold searches the six tuning projects, as the benchmark did. It picks depth 4, 200 rounds, a learning rate of 0.05, `min_child_weight` 5 and `lambda` 10, and its AUROC on HOLZ, 0.79, is the benchmark's XGBoost score on HOLZ. The seven searches picked seven different settings. The seven estimates run from 0.70 on RPP to 0.86 on ML1, and `summary()` gives a mean of 0.78, an SD of 0.06 and a `lower` of 0.73. AdaBoost's nested search of the full grid, the dataset `nested` of Module 9, gives a mean of 0.76, an SD of 0.12 and a `lower` of 0.64. So XGBoost's procedure scores a little higher on average and varies less across projects. The two searches differ in grid and rule, and seven projects cannot make these differences firm. The box needs the xgboost package. It runs in about 75 seconds on four cores.

```{r benchmark-xgb}
# Four hyperparameters crossed with five numbers of rounds
xgb_hgrid <- expand.grid(
  depth = c(1, 2, 4),
  eta = c(0.1, 0.05, 0.01),
  min_child_weight = c(1, 5),
  lambda = c(1, 10),
  n_iter = c(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
)

# The recipe: the grid sets its hyperparameters; its own data play no part
xgb_fit <- xgboost::xgboost(
  x = df_noholz[, pred_nms],
  y = df_noholz[, out_nme],
  nthreads = 1
)

# Nested LOGO-CV on all seven projects, each search by XGBoost's own rule
xgb_nested <- tune_logo_cv(
  xgb_fit,
  xgb_hgrid,
  data = df,
  group = "pid",
  outcome = out_nme,
  nested = TRUE,
  sort_by = c("min", "lower"),
  cores = 4
)
xgb_nested
summary(xgb_nested)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The adatutor package is a teaching package. It accompanies this tutorial and serves readers who explore AdaBoost, cross-validation, and a little beyond. Its functions are small on purpose: each folds one step that the tutorial first builds by hand, so readers can focus on one piece at a time. The package does not claim to be complete. For applied work, a full machine-learning infrastructure such as tidymodels [@tidymodels] is the better home. It offers cross-validation, bootstraps, and nested folds through `rsample` [@rsample], many more models through `parsnip`, and tuning workflows around them. The move is short, because adatutor follows the same conventions: `initial_split()` takes the same `prop` and `strata` arguments as `partition()`, models are fitted with a formula and a data frame, and predictions come from `predict()` with a `type` argument.
:::

#### Listing [NEW]

Search the XGBoost grid by project with tidymodels (under a minute).

```{r listing-tidymodels}
# Install once: install.packages("tidymodels")
library(tidymodels)

# The model: XGBoost, with four hyperparameters left open for tuning
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(
  tree_depth = tune(),
  learn_rate = tune(),
  min_n = tune(),
  trees = tune()
) |>
  set_engine("xgboost", event_level = "second") |>
  set_mode("classification")

# The workflow: the predictors and outcome of Listing 3, and the model
xgb_wflow <- workflow(reformulate(pred_nms, out_nme), xgb_spec)

# The folds: one per project, as in Module 6
folds <- group_vfold_cv(df_noholz, group = pid)

# The grid: the settings of the XGBoost box at its default penalty
xgb_hgrid_tm <- expand.grid(
  tree_depth = c(1, 2, 4),
  learn_rate = c(0.1, 0.05, 0.01),
  min_n = c(1, 5),
  trees = c(50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
)

# The search: LOGO-CV for every setting, scored by the AUROC
xgb_tune_tm <- tune_grid(
  xgb_wflow,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = xgb_hgrid_tm,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
  control = control_grid(event_level = "second")
)

# The AUROC of every setting on every project
collect_metrics(xgb_tune_tm, summarize = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
The workflow of this tutorial carries over to tidymodels. Listing [NEW] writes the XGBoost search as a model specification: `boost_tree()` names the model, `tune()` marks the hyperparameters to search, and `set_engine()` picks the implementation. With the bonsai package loaded, `set_engine("lightgbm")` runs the same search in LightGBM. CatBoost is available in the same way, but its settings need care: `min_n`, for example, has no effect under its default trees. `group_vfold_cv()` builds one fold per project, the LOGO-CV of Module 6, and `tune_grid()` scores every setting on every fold. `collect_metrics()` then returns the AUROC of every setting on every project, as `tune_logo_cv()` does, and the rule of Module 7 applies to these values unchanged. @kuhn2023 explain the framework step by step.

One step has no ready-made function. The framework builds nested folds, but its tuning functions do not run the nested search, so readers write the outer loop themselves. Readers of Module 9 know how: hold out a project, search on the rest, fit the winner, score the project. That is what building the workflow by hand is for. Each piece can be handed to a framework once it is understood, and what a framework lacks can still be written.
:::

- New listing for R1.C3 ("the tidymodels stack with parsnip/workflows"). It ran on this machine on 20 Nov in 38 s (tidymodels with xgboost; six tuning projects, HOLZ not scored).
- Agreement with the package, same 90 settings at `lambda` 1: 475 of 540 AUROCs are identical to `tune_logo_cv()`; 65 differ (median 0.007, at most 0.048). Two causes explain all 65, found and checked independently on 20 Nov; ties are not one of them. (1) 63 cells: for `trees` below the largest value of the grid, parsnip 1.6.1 with xgboost 3.2.1.1 predicts from one round too many (`trees = 50` scores 51 rounds). (2) 2 cells: parsnip fits the first outcome level by default, and `control_grid(event_level = "second")` changes only the metric; the mirrored fit drifts in the last digits over hundreds of rounds. The listing now sets `set_engine("xgboost", event_level = "second")` (author, 22 Nov), which removes cause (2); cause (1) stays, so 63 cells still differ. With one `trees` value per run on top, all 540 held-out scores are bit-identical to the package. The text therefore says "as `tune_logo_cv()` does", not "the same numbers".
- `lambda` is an engine argument in parsnip and stays at its default, so the listing searches 90 settings, not the 180 of the XGBoost box. `min_n` is XGBoost's `min_child_weight`.
- `event_level = "second"` is needed: "success" is the second level of the outcome. Without it every AUROC is one minus the right value.
- LightGBM and CatBoost engines, tested 20 Nov on the six tuning projects (lightgbm 4.7.0, catboost 1.2.10, bonsai 0.4.1; Mac only). Both need `library(bonsai)` besides the `set_engine()` line, so the Add box no longer says "changes one line" (reworded 22 Nov, author). LightGBM: runs unchanged, no warnings, results repeat. CatBoost: not on CRAN (GitHub release); ignores `min_n` under its default symmetric trees, without a warning; results change with the seed; below 200 trees the search scores the first trees of a longer fit, which is not the model a fit at that size gives. `min_n` maps to `min_child_weight` in XGBoost but to `min_data_in_leaf` in LightGBM and CatBoost.
- parsnip has no AdaBoost engine (checked in its documentation on 20 Nov), so the listing cannot show AdaBoost by switching the engine.
- Bib key `kuhn2023` is new in the vignette bib. It cites the online book (author, 20 Nov): authors, title, URL and "Version 1.0.0 (2023-09-06)" were read on tmwr.org. Chapter 15, "Screening Many Models", covers workflow sets.
:::

Why AdaBoost, then? No algorithm wins on every problem [@wolpert1997]. With the small samples and noisy predictors of psychology, simpler models often match more flexible ones [@speck2026]. The aim of this tutorial was to learn one algorithm from the inside, on a real and hard problem, not to win a benchmark. AdaBoost serves that aim. It is simple enough to build by hand, and it holds its own against the alternatives.

XGBoost is the next place to go. It boosts trees by gradient steps, as the Conclusion explains, and it adds two regularizers that AdaBoost lacks. `min_child_weight` blocks a split that would leave a leaf with too little data. `lambda` shrinks the leaf values toward zero, an L2 penalty. On the six tuning projects, in the search behind `benchmark` (`data-raw/benchmark.R`), XGBoost has the higher floor, the score on the hardest projects. By the highest `lower`, the best of its 180 settings beats the best of AdaBoost's 1,320 (0.71 against 0.67). By the best worst project, its grid beats AdaBoost's as well (0.71 against 0.68). The first regularizer seems to matter: the ten XGBoost settings with the highest `lower`, and the ten with the best worst project, all set `min_child_weight` to 5. The second shows no clear pattern: at `lambda` 1 and at 10, the best `lower` and the best worst project differ by less than 0.01. The higher floor, not the score on HOLZ, is the reason to move on. The same search runs in [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org), the framework the rsample package of Listing 10 belongs to. The comparison is not fully even, though: XGBoost was tuned over five hyperparameters, AdaBoost over three.

Note: Min child weight in xgb can be emulated with minbucket (round(minsplit / 3) about 7)
minsplit: minimum number of observations that must exist in a parent node before `rpart` we attempt a split

# Conclusion

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial"}
Is adaboost a contemporary algorithm? No. It is indeed largely superseeded by more general and flexible(?) algorithms such as gradient boosting and XGBoost. Is it still worth learning/have at ones disposal? From our perspective, yes. Adaboost is a bridge into the world of boosting algorithms.
AdaBoost is forward stagewise additive modeling with exponential loss. So if readers are willing to futher engage with loss functions, they can swap the exponential loss for log loss and get LogitBoost. And then they can appreciate that the log loss gives calibrated probabilities, instead of margins. For replication prediction, a probability might be a tempting additional. If readers are then ready to swap the loss for any differentiable loss and
take gradients instead of reweighting and they have gradient boosting. If they are ready to add second derivative information they can switch to newtonboosting and get pretty close to XGBoost.
Readers who built AdaBoost by hand are the only audience that can follow that derivation and appreciate the gained benefits of the extensions with code, and it’s the step that turns “AdaBoost is old” into **“AdaBoost is the simplest case of what you’ll use”**. And we want swap regression out of our toolbox, only because xxx exists.


AdaBoost is also the simplest member of the boosting family that applied work uses today. Friedman et al. [-@friedman2000] showed that AdaBoost fits an additive model one stump at a time, and that each round minimizes an exponential loss: the observation weights of Module 3 are, up to a sign, the gradient of that loss. Replacing the exponential loss by the log loss gives LogitBoost, which returns probabilities instead of margins. Replacing the reweighting by a gradient step on any differentiable loss gives gradient boosting [@friedman2001], TODO add 2nd d infor: newton boosting the algorithm behind XGBoost [@chen2016]. Readers who built AdaBoost by hand in Module 3 have therefore built the skeleton of all of them: a weak learner, T rounds, a learning rate, and a loss that decides what the next round corrects.

The example also shows a limit that no algorithm removes. @altmejd2019 already called their data "arguably too small" (p. 2). Our results locate the problem: with seven replication projects, the spread across projects is far larger than any difference between settings or models. Machine learning on replication outcomes therefore needs more projects, not only more study effects: each new large-scale replication project adds a fold to the cross-validation and a test for the next model. Larger datasets with replication attempts nested in study effects and projects would support estimates at both levels.
:::

# Appendix B: Trees by Hand

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix)"}
**A tree, unfolded.** The modules leave the stumps and trees of AdaBoost to `rpart()`. This appendix grows a tree by hand instead, one question at a time. A stump is this tree at depth 1: with `D <- D1` and `max_depth <- 1`, the listing asks the question of the first stump in Listing 19.

To find a question, the listing tries every predictor and every midpoint between neighboring values, as Listing 14 did for power. For each split, it computes the Gini impurity of Module 2, with the weights in place of the counts. It keeps the split if it is purer than the best so far.

A tree runs this search in every node, one level at a time. All study effects start in node 1, the root. A split of node k sends each study effect to node 2k (below the cut) or to node 2k + 1 (at or above it).

The listing copies two defaults of `rpart()`. It skips a split that leaves fewer than 7 study effects on one side (`minbucket`), and it does not split a node with fewer than 20 (`minsplit`). For the comparison, we tell `rpart()` to keep every split (`cp = -1`). By default, it drops a split that lowers the error too little: for a stump, by less than 1 percent of the root's error.

Grow a tree of depth 3 under the weights of round 2 in Listing 24, with every step by hand (under a second).

```{r tree-craft}
# The weights after round 1 (Listing 23), and the maximum depth
D <- D2
max_depth <- 3

# Every study effect starts in node 1, the root
node_train <- rep(1, m)

# The questions of the tree, one row per split
tree_craft <- data.frame(
  node = numeric(),
  pred_nme = character(),
  cut = numeric()
)

# Split one level at a time
for (level in seq_len(max_depth)) {
  # The nodes of this level: 1 at level 1, 2 and 3 at level 2, 4 to 7 at
  # level 3, and so on
  nodes <- sort(unique(node_train[node_train >= 2^(level - 1)]))
  for (k in nodes) {
    in_node <- node_train == k
    # rpart's default: no split for fewer than 20 study effects (minsplit)
    if (sum(in_node) < 20) {
      next
    }
    # The impurity to beat: the weighted Gini impurity of node k itself
    y_k <- y_train[in_node]
    D_k <- D[in_node]
    p <- sum(D_k[y_k == "success"]) / sum(D_k)
    gini_best <- 1 - (p^2 + (1 - p)^2)
    pred_best <- NA
    # Every predictor, and every midpoint between neighboring values, as in
    # Listing 14
    for (pred_nme in pred_nms) {
      x <- train[[pred_nme]][in_node]
      values <- sort(unique(x))
      cuts <- (values[-1] + values[-length(values)]) / 2
      for (cut in cuts) {
        left <- x < cut
        # rpart's default: at least 7 study effects on each side (minbucket)
        if (sum(left) < 7 || sum(!left) < 7) {
          next
        }
        # The weight on each side, and its weighted share of successes
        w_left <- sum(D_k[left])
        w_right <- sum(D_k[!left])
        p_left <- sum(D_k[left & y_k == "success"]) / w_left
        p_right <- sum(D_k[!left & y_k == "success"]) / w_right
        # The Gini impurity of each side and of the split, as in Module 2,
        # with weights in place of counts
        gini_left <- 1 - (p_left^2 + (1 - p_left)^2)
        gini_right <- 1 - (p_right^2 + (1 - p_right)^2)
        gini_split <- (w_left * gini_left + w_right * gini_right) / sum(D_k)
        # Keep the question if it is purer than the best so far
        if (gini_split < gini_best) {
          gini_best <- gini_split
          pred_best <- pred_nme
          cut_best <- cut
        }
      }
    }
    # No split makes node k purer: it stays a leaf
    if (is.na(pred_best)) {
      next
    }
    # Store the question; send the study effects to nodes 2k and 2k + 1
    tree_craft[nrow(tree_craft) + 1, ] <- list(k, pred_best, cut_best)
    node_train[in_node] <- ifelse(
      train[[pred_best]][in_node] < cut_best,
      2 * k,
      2 * k + 1
    )
  }
}
tree_craft

# Each leaf predicts the class that carries more than half of its weight
p_leaf <- tapply(D * (y_train == "success"), node_train, sum) /
  tapply(D, node_train, sum)
leaf_class <- ifelse(p_leaf > 0.5, "success", "failure")
leaf_class

# The number of study effects in each leaf
table(node_train)

# Retrodictions: the class of the leaf each study effect ends in
y_retro_craft <- as.vector(leaf_class[as.character(node_train)])

# Predictions: replay the stored questions on the test set, from the root down
node_test <- rep(1, nrow(test))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(tree_craft))) {
  k <- tree_craft$node[i]
  in_node <- node_test == k
  node_test[in_node] <- ifelse(
    test[[tree_craft$pred_nme[i]]][in_node] < tree_craft$cut[i],
    2 * k,
    2 * k + 1
  )
}
y_pred_craft <- as.vector(leaf_class[as.character(node_test)])

# Verification: rpart's tree with the same weights and depth, told to keep
# every split (cp = -1) and to skip its internal cross-validation (xval = 0)
tree_rpart <- rpart::rpart(
  replicate ~ .,
  data = train[, voi_nms],
  method = "class",
  maxdepth = max_depth,
  weights = D,
  cp = -1,
  xval = 0
)
y_retro_rpart <- as.character(
  predict(tree_rpart, newdata = train[, pred_nms], type = "class")
)
y_pred_rpart <- as.character(
  predict(tree_rpart, newdata = test[, pred_nms], type = "class")
)

# The same number of splits, the same retrodictions and test predictions
nrow(tree_craft) == sum(tree_rpart$frame$var != "<leaf>")
identical(y_retro_craft, y_retro_rpart)
identical(y_pred_craft, y_pred_rpart)

# The first question is the stump of round 2 in Listing 24
tree_craft$pred_nme[1] == ada_diy$t2$h$frame$var[1]
all.equal(tree_craft$cut[1], ada_diy$t2$h$splits[1, "index"])
```

Under `D2`, the weights that round 2 of Listing 24 fits its stump to, the first question is that stump: power at 0.547. Three more questions follow. Node 5 stays a leaf because it holds 19 study effects, one short of `minsplit`. Each leaf predicts the class that carries more than half of its weight, and all predictions match those of `rpart()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix, decide at port)"}
**The same tree as functions.** We can also write the loop as four short functions. `measure_impurity()` and `find_split()` search one node, and `grow_tree()` splits it and calls itself on each side, one level shallower. `predict_tree()` follows the questions down to a leaf. At depth 1 under `D1`, the functions ask the question of the first stump in Listing 19; at depth 3 under `D2`, they grow the tree above.

Write the tree search as functions, and grow the first stump of Listing 19 and the tree above with them (under a second).

```{r tree-diy}
# The weighted Gini impurity of a group of study effects, as in Module 2
measure_impurity <- function(y, w) {
  p <- sum(w[y == "success"]) / sum(w)
  1 - (p^2 + (1 - p)^2)
}

# The purest question for a group of study effects: the search inside the
# loop above, over every predictor and every midpoint
find_split <- function(x, y, w) {
  gini_best <- measure_impurity(y, w)
  pred_best <- NA
  cut_best <- NA
  for (pred_nme in names(x)) {
    values <- sort(unique(x[[pred_nme]]))
    cuts <- (values[-1] + values[-length(values)]) / 2
    for (cut in cuts) {
      left <- x[[pred_nme]] < cut
      # rpart's default: at least 7 study effects on each side (minbucket)
      if (sum(left) < 7 || sum(!left) < 7) {
        next
      }
      w_left <- sum(w[left])
      w_right <- sum(w[!left])
      gini_left <- measure_impurity(y[left], w[left])
      gini_right <- measure_impurity(y[!left], w[!left])
      gini_split <- (w_left * gini_left + w_right * gini_right) / sum(w)
      if (gini_split < gini_best) {
        gini_best <- gini_split
        pred_best <- pred_nme
        cut_best <- cut
      }
    }
  }
  list(pred_nme = pred_best, cut = cut_best)
}

# A tree: the purest question, then a tree one level shallower on each side
grow_tree <- function(x, y, w, max_depth) {
  # A leaf predicts the class that carries more than half of its weight
  p_success <- sum(w[y == "success"]) / sum(w)
  leaf <- list(class = if (p_success > 0.5) "success" else "failure")
  # rpart's default: no split for fewer than 20 study effects (minsplit)
  if (max_depth == 0 || length(y) < 20) {
    return(leaf)
  }
  question <- find_split(x, y, w)
  # No split makes the group purer: it stays a leaf
  if (is.na(question[["pred_nme"]])) {
    return(leaf)
  }
  left <- x[[question[["pred_nme"]]]] < question[["cut"]]
  list(
    pred_nme = question[["pred_nme"]],
    cut = question[["cut"]],
    left = grow_tree(x[left, ], y[left], w[left], max_depth - 1),
    right = grow_tree(x[!left, ], y[!left], w[!left], max_depth - 1)
  )
}

# The class of each study effect: follow the questions down to a leaf
predict_tree <- function(tree, x) {
  # A leaf: every study effect that reaches it gets its class
  if (is.null(tree[["pred_nme"]])) {
    return(rep(tree[["class"]], nrow(x)))
  }
  left <- x[[tree[["pred_nme"]]]] < tree[["cut"]]
  y_pred <- character(nrow(x))
  y_pred[left] <- predict_tree(tree[["left"]], x[left, ])
  y_pred[!left] <- predict_tree(tree[["right"]], x[!left, ])
  y_pred
}

# Depth 1 under the equal weights D1: a stump, and its question
stump_diy <- grow_tree(train[, pred_nms], y_train, D1, max_depth = 1)
stump_diy[c("pred_nme", "cut")]

# Depth 3 under D2: the tree of the loop above
tree_diy <- grow_tree(train[, pred_nms], y_train, D2, max_depth = 3)

# Verification: the question of the first stump h1, Listing 19
stump_diy[["pred_nme"]] == h1$frame$var[1]
all.equal(stump_diy[["cut"]], h1$splits[1, "index"])

# Verification: the retrodictions and test predictions of tree_craft and of
# rpart's tree
identical(predict_tree(tree_diy, train[, pred_nms]), y_retro_craft)
identical(predict_tree(tree_diy, test[, pred_nms]), y_pred_craft)
identical(predict_tree(tree_diy, train[, pred_nms]), y_retro_rpart)
identical(predict_tree(tree_diy, test[, pred_nms]), y_pred_rpart)
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
- **Verified.** All 5 checks of `tree-craft` print `TRUE` after Listing 31 (adatutor 1.0.0 from source, rpart 4.1.27). Under weights of 1, `D1`, `D2`, the round-10 weights of Listing 24 and random weights, at depths 1 to 5, all 25 trees matched `rpart()` in questions, leaves and predictions.
- **Defaults.** The listing copies `minsplit = 20` and `minbucket = 7` from `rpart.control()`. The check tree keeps every split with `cp = -1`, and `xval = 0` only skips rpart's cross-validation: with `xval = 10`, the tree is the same.
- **The 1 percent rule.** The prose states rpart's default `cp` rule for stumps, which a reader who pastes the loop into Listing 24 needs. With the rule, a by-hand AdaBoost loop reproduces all 1,000 model weights of Listing 24 and its 97 rounds without a split (Module 4).
- **Ties.** In an exact tie, the loop keeps the first split in the order of `pred_nms` and the cuts, while `rpart()` keeps the one its own arithmetic rounds higher. This changed the split in 23 of 1,200 trees under random weights (depths 1 to 4): the retrodictions always matched, and the test predictions differed in 6.
- **Node numbers.** `rpart()` also numbers nodes 2k and 2k + 1, but may send the side at or above the cut to 2k, as `h1` does with `p_value.o >= 0.000656632`. The numbers differed in 24 of the 25 trees above, but the questions, leaves and predictions did not.
- **Leaf probabilities.** Under weights that sum to 1, the class probabilities of `rpart()` differ from the weighted shares, by up to 0.42 in these runs (success at `h1`'s root: 0.450, not 0.475). The cause is a line in `rpart()` (rpart 4.1.27) that scales each class by `prior / pmax(1, counts)`, with `counts` the class weight totals, so totals below 1 count as 1.
- **Classes.** This formula reproduced rpart's probabilities in all 1,225 trees, but `predict(type = "class")` reads the class from `frame$yval`, not from these probabilities. The leaf classes matched the listing's in all 1,225 trees, and AdaBoost uses only the classes.
- **Not verified.** A leaf with exactly half its weight on successes, where the listing predicts failure (no leaf in these runs came closer than 0.00012). Also: missing predictor values, predictors that are not numeric, depths above 5, other data, and the `cp` rule inside deeper trees.
- **Function version (cut with its box).** All 6 checks of `tree-diy` print `TRUE`. The functions break ties as the loop does and matched its questions, retrodictions and test predictions in all 1,225 trees.
- **Open pointer.** Module 2's "TODO: Moving beyond classification stump Add trees" can point to this appendix.
:::

# Appendix C: The AUROC by Hand

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix)"}
**The AUROC, unfolded.** The modules use `auroc()` without building it first; this appendix builds it. Module 6 defined the AUROC as the chance that a randomly drawn success scores higher than a randomly drawn failure. The listing counts this chance directly. It compares every success in the test set with every failure, and takes the share of pairs in which the success has the higher margin; a tie counts as half.

No threshold enters, which separates the AUROC from the balanced accuracy. On the class labels, every score is -1 or 1. The labels then rank a pair correctly only if the ensemble predicts the success as success and the failure as failure. A pair with the same label on both sides is a tie.

Counting each tie as half turns the share into the balanced accuracy: 0.61 on our test set, where 117 of the 240 pairs are ties. On the margin, no pair is a tie, and the AUROC is 0.70.

Compute the AUROC of Listing 31 by hand, on the margin and on the class labels (under a second).

```{r auroc-craft}
# The AUROC by hand: the share of success-failure pairs that the margin
# ranks correctly; a tie counts as half
mgn_success <- y_pred_mgn[y_test == "success"]
mgn_failure <- y_pred_mgn[y_test == "failure"]
mgn_diff <- outer(mgn_success, mgn_failure, "-")
auc_craft <- mean((mgn_diff > 0) + 0.5 * (mgn_diff == 0))
auc_craft

# One row per success, one column per failure: every pair once
dim(mgn_diff)

# The same four lines on the class labels
cls_success <- y_pred_cls[y_test == "success"]
cls_failure <- y_pred_cls[y_test == "failure"]
cls_diff <- outer(cls_success, cls_failure, "-")
auc_cls_craft <- mean((cls_diff > 0) + 0.5 * (cls_diff == 0))
auc_cls_craft

# The number of tied pairs, on the margin and on the class labels
sum(mgn_diff == 0)
sum(cls_diff == 0)

# Verification: auroc() on the margin
all.equal(auc_craft, auroc(y_test, y_pred_mgn))

# Verification: on the class labels, the balanced accuracy of Listing 31 and
# auroc() on the labels
all.equal(auc_cls_craft, (sens + spec) / 2)
all.equal(auc_cls_craft, auroc(y_test, y_pred_cls))
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check in tutorial"}
- **Verified.** All 3 checks print `TRUE` after Listing 31 and its package solution (adatutor 1.0.0 from source), also with the trees appendix run first. On the margin, the 240 pairs of 15 successes and 16 failures give 0.7 by hand, from `auroc()` and from `PRROC::roc.curve()`, with no tied pairs.
- **On the class labels.** The by-hand share, `auroc(y_test, y_pred_cls)` and `(sens + spec) / 2` all give 0.6104167, with 117 tied pairs. Sensitivity is 8 of 15 and specificity 11 of 16: 88 pairs right, 40 + 77 = 117 ties, and 35 wrong.
- **Why the labels give the balanced accuracy.** The share is `(TP * TN + 0.5 * (TP * FP + FN * TN)) / (P * N)`, which equals `(sens + spec) / 2` for any labels. The algebra is ours, and the numbers come from the run.
- **Not verified.** Data other than this test set, missing margins or labels (none here), and run time and memory on large data, where `outer()` builds one cell per pair.
:::

# Appendix D: The Grid Search by Hand

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix)"}
The listings of the modules fold earlier steps into function calls. Appendices D and E unfold them: the same searches, with every step written out.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix)"}
**The same search, unfolded.** Listing 34 folds the steps of the earlier modules into three calls. Unfolded one layer, the search is the fold loop of Listing 32 inside the loop over the grid. Unfolded all the way, it is that loop around the boosting rounds of Listing 24 and the margin of Listing 28, with the AUROC of Listing 31 at the end. Nothing else changes, and the 18 rows come out the same both times, to the digit.

One layer out: the LOGO-CV of Listing 32 written out in place of `logo_cv()` (about 2 minutes).

```{r listing-34-diy}
# The grid again, with the LOGO-CV of Listing 32 written out in place of
# logo_cv()
ada_hgrid_diy <- ada_hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]
ada_hgrid_diy[proj_nms] <- NA_real_
for (i in seq_len(nrow(ada_hgrid_diy))) {
  for (rp in proj_nms) {
    # Training and test set
    test_cv <- df_split[[rp]]
    train_cv <- df_noholz[df_noholz$pid != rp, ]
    # The weak learner at this depth, boosted at this setting
    h_cv <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train_cv[, voi_nms],
      method = "class",
      maxdepth = ada_hgrid_diy$depth[i],
      parms = list(split = "gini"),
      model = TRUE
    )
    ada_cv <- h_cv |>
      adaboost(
        n_iter = ada_hgrid_diy$n_iter[i],
        eta = ada_hgrid_diy$eta[i],
        verbose = FALSE
      )
    # The AUROC of the held-out project, scored on the margin
    y_cv <- predict(
      ada_cv,
      newdata = test_cv[, pred_nms],
      type = "margin",
      verbose = FALSE
    )
    ada_hgrid_diy[[rp]][i] <- auroc(test_cv[, out_nme], y_cv)
  }
}

# The same 18 by 6 AUROCs as Listing 34
all.equal(ada_hgrid_diy[proj_nms], ada_hgrid[proj_nms])
```

All layers out: the boosting rounds of Listing 24 and the margin of Listing 28 pasted in as well (about 3 minutes).

"Its all in the loop"

```{r listing-34-craft}
# The grid again, with the by-hand steps of Modules 2, 3, 5 and 6 pasted
# into the loop over the settings
ada_hgrid_craft <- ada_hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]
ada_hgrid_craft[proj_nms] <- NA_real_
for (i in seq_len(nrow(ada_hgrid_craft))) {
  # Module 6, Listing 32: each project is the test set once
  for (rp in proj_nms) {
    test_cv <- df_split[[rp]]
    train_cv <- df_noholz[df_noholz$pid != rp, ]
    y_train_cv <- train_cv[, out_nme]
    m_cv <- nrow(train_cv)
    # Module 3, Listing 24: the boosting rounds at this setting, the tree of
    # Module 2, Listing 12 at this depth
    ada_cv <- vector("list", ada_hgrid_craft$n_iter[i])
    D <- rep(1, m_cv) / m_cv
    for (t in seq_len(ada_hgrid_craft$n_iter[i])) {
      h <- rpart::rpart(
        replicate ~ .,
        data = train_cv[, voi_nms],
        method = "class",
        maxdepth = ada_hgrid_craft$depth[i],
        weights = D
      )
      y_retro <- predict(h, newdata = train_cv[, pred_nms], type = "class")
      epsilon <- sum(D * (y_retro != y_train_cv))
      alpha <- 0.5 * log((1 - epsilon) / epsilon) * ada_hgrid_craft$eta[i]
      chi <- (y_retro == y_train_cv) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train_cv) * -1
      D_raw <- D * exp(-alpha * chi)
      D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)
      ada_cv[[t]] <- list(h = h, alpha = alpha)
    }
    # Module 5, Listing 28: the margin on the held-out project
    h_cv <- lapply(ada_cv, "[[", "h")
    alpha_cv <- sapply(ada_cv, "[[", "alpha")
    y_pred_cstp <- sapply(
      h_cv,
      predict,
      newdata = test_cv[, pred_nms],
      type = "vector"
    )
    y_pred_1m1 <- 2 * y_pred_cstp - 3
    pred_mgn_cv <- as.vector(alpha_cv %*% t(y_pred_1m1))
    # Module 6, Listing 31: the AUROC of the held-out project
    ada_hgrid_craft[[rp]][i] <- auroc(test_cv[, out_nme], pred_mgn_cv)
  }
}

# The same 18 by 6 AUROCs as Listing 34
all.equal(ada_hgrid_craft[proj_nms], ada_hgrid[proj_nms])
```
:::

# Appendix E: The Nested Search by Hand

::: {.callout-note title="Add to tutorial (appendix)"}
**The nested search, unfolded.** Listing 36 folds the inner search into `tune_logo_cv()`, the pick into `summary()`, and the refit into `logo_cv()`. Unfolded all the way, the search and the refit are the by-hand steps of Appendix D: the boosting rounds of Listing 24 and the margin of Listing 28, with the AUROC of Listing 31 at the end. The pick computes `lower` by hand, as Listing 34 did, and takes the setting with the highest. The listing runs them once for every setting and inner project, and once more for each winner on all six projects. The seven estimates and the seven winners come out the same as in Listing 36.

Run the same nested cross-validation with every step by hand (about 24 minutes).

```{r listing-36-craft}
# The nested search of Listing 36 again, with the by-hand steps of Modules 2,
# 3, 5 and 6 pasted into the loops
auc_nested_craft <- setNames(rep(NA_real_, length(proj_all)), proj_all)
winners_craft <- list()
# Outer loop: each project is held out once and scored once
for (rp in proj_all) {
  # Progress report, overwritten in place
  cat("\rHeld-out project:", rp)
  # The held-out project leaves the data, so the search cannot see it
  train_cv <- df[df$pid != rp, ]
  test_cv <- df[df$pid == rp, ]
  # Module 7: the grid search of Listing 34 on the other six projects
  proj_inner <- setdiff(proj_all, rp)
  ada_hgrid_inner <- ada_hgrid[, c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")]
  ada_hgrid_inner[proj_inner] <- NA_real_
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(ada_hgrid_inner))) {
    # Module 6, Listing 32: each of the six is the inner test set once
    for (ip in proj_inner) {
      test_inner <- train_cv[train_cv$pid == ip, ]
      train_inner <- train_cv[train_cv$pid != ip, ]
      y_train_inner <- train_inner[, out_nme]
      m_inner <- nrow(train_inner)
      # Module 3, Listing 24: the boosting rounds at this setting, the tree of
      # Module 2, Listing 12 at this depth
      ada_inner <- vector("list", ada_hgrid_inner$n_iter[i])
      D <- rep(1, m_inner) / m_inner
      for (t in seq_len(ada_hgrid_inner$n_iter[i])) {
        h <- rpart::rpart(
          replicate ~ .,
          data = train_inner[, voi_nms],
          method = "class",
          maxdepth = ada_hgrid_inner$depth[i],
          weights = D
        )
        y_retro <- predict(h, newdata = train_inner[, pred_nms], type = "class")
        epsilon <- sum(D * (y_retro != y_train_inner))
        alpha <- 0.5 * log((1 - epsilon) / epsilon) * ada_hgrid_inner$eta[i]
        chi <- (y_retro == y_train_inner) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train_inner) * -1
        D_raw <- D * exp(-alpha * chi)
        D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)
        ada_inner[[t]] <- list(h = h, alpha = alpha)
      }
      # Module 5, Listing 28: the margin on the inner held-out project
      h_inner <- lapply(ada_inner, "[[", "h")
      alpha_inner <- sapply(ada_inner, "[[", "alpha")
      y_pred_cstp <- sapply(
        h_inner,
        predict,
        newdata = test_inner[, pred_nms],
        type = "vector"
      )
      y_pred_1m1 <- 2 * y_pred_cstp - 3
      pred_mgn_inner <- as.vector(alpha_inner %*% t(y_pred_1m1))
      # Module 6, Listing 31: the AUROC of the inner held-out project
      ada_hgrid_inner[[ip]][i] <- auroc(test_inner[, out_nme], pred_mgn_inner)
    }
  }
  # The winner: the highest lower, the mean over the inner folds minus their SD
  auc_inner <- as.matrix(ada_hgrid_inner[proj_inner])
  lower_inner <- rowMeans(auc_inner) - apply(auc_inner, 1, sd)
  winners_craft[[rp]] <- ada_hgrid[
    which.max(lower_inner),
    c("depth", "n_iter", "eta")
  ]
  # Module 3, Listing 24 again: the winning setting, boosted on all six projects
  y_train_cv <- train_cv[, out_nme]
  m_cv <- nrow(train_cv)
  ada_cv <- vector("list", winners_craft[[rp]]$n_iter)
  D <- rep(1, m_cv) / m_cv
  for (t in seq_len(winners_craft[[rp]]$n_iter)) {
    h <- rpart::rpart(
      replicate ~ .,
      data = train_cv[, voi_nms],
      method = "class",
      maxdepth = winners_craft[[rp]]$depth,
      weights = D
    )
    y_retro <- predict(h, newdata = train_cv[, pred_nms], type = "class")
    epsilon <- sum(D * (y_retro != y_train_cv))
    alpha <- 0.5 * log((1 - epsilon) / epsilon) * winners_craft[[rp]]$eta
    chi <- (y_retro == y_train_cv) * 1 + (y_retro != y_train_cv) * -1
    D_raw <- D * exp(-alpha * chi)
    D <- D_raw / sum(D_raw)
    ada_cv[[t]] <- list(h = h, alpha = alpha)
  }
  # Module 5, Listing 28 again: the margin on the held-out project
  h_cv <- lapply(ada_cv, "[[", "h")
  alpha_cv <- sapply(ada_cv, "[[", "alpha")
  y_pred_cstp <- sapply(
    h_cv,
    predict,
    newdata = test_cv[, pred_nms],
    type = "vector"
  )
  y_pred_1m1 <- 2 * y_pred_cstp - 3
  pred_mgn_cv <- as.vector(alpha_cv %*% t(y_pred_1m1))
  # Module 6, Listing 31 again: the held-out project, scored once
  auc_nested_craft[[rp]] <- auroc(test_cv[, out_nme], pred_mgn_cv)
}

# The same seven AUROCs as Listing 36
all.equal(auc_nested_craft, auc_nested_diy)

# The same seven winners as Listing 36
identical(do.call(rbind, winners_craft), do.call(rbind, winners_diy))
```
